statement: For random vectors $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_m)^{\mathrm{T}}$ and $\mathbf{Y} = (Y_1, \dots, Y_n)^{\mathrm{T}}$, the cross-covariance matrix $\operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}} = \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y})$ is the $m \times n$ matrix whose $(i, j)$-th entry is $\operatorname{cov}(X_i, Y_j) = \operatorname{E}[(X_i - \operatorname{E}[X_i])(Y_j - \operatorname{E}[Y_j])]$. In matrix notation, $\operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}) = \operatorname{E}[(\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{X}})(\mathbf{Y} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{Y}})^{\mathrm{T}}]$ for real random vectors, and $\operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}} = \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{W}) = \operatorname{E}[(\mathbf{Z} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}})(\mathbf{W} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{W}})^{\mathrm{H}}]$ for complex random vectors.

symbols.meaning: Cross-covariance matrix of X and Y, denoted \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y})
symbols.dimensions: m x n (or p x q)

symbols.meaning: The i-th component random variable of X
The j-th component random variable of Y

properties.why: Expansion of centered product and linearity of expectation
Transpose of an outer product reverses vector order
Distributivity of matrix multiplication and linearity of expectation
Constants subtract out in centering and matrix factors factor out of expectation

properties.property: If \mathbf{X} and \mathbf{Y} are independent (or every component of \mathbf{X} is uncorrelated with every component of \mathbf{Y}), \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}) = 0_{p \times q}
properties.why: Expectations factor for uncorrelated centered components
Expansion of the variance of a vector sum

properties.property: The joint covariance matrix partitions as \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{bmatrix} \operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}} & \operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}} \\ \operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{X}} & \operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{Y}} \end{bmatrix}
properties.why: Off-diagonal blocks of joint covariance matrix are cross-covariance matrices

properties.property: For complex vectors, \operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}} = \operatorname{E}[(\mathbf{Z} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}})(\mathbf{W} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{W}})^{\mathrm{H}}] and pseudo-cross-covariance is \operatorname{J}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}} = \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{Z}, \overline{\mathbf{W}}) = \operatorname{E}[(\mathbf{Z} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{Z}})(\mathbf{W} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{W}})^{\mathrm{T}}]
properties.why: Transposition is replaced by Hermitian transposition in complex vector spaces

assumptions.assumption: All component random variables of X and Y have finite first and second moments
assumptions.breaks_when: The underlying distributions are heavy-tailed (e.g., Cauchy) such that means or expectations of cross-products do not exist or diverge

assumptions.assumption: X and Y are finite-dimensional random vectors
assumptions.breaks_when: Infinite-dimensional stochastic processes without well-defined matrix representations

failure_modes.signature: Matrix entries evaluate to NaN or diverge to infinity
failure_modes.cause: Non-existent or infinite first or second moments for components of X or Y

failure_modes.signature: Dimension incompatibility error when substituting cov(X, Y) for cov(Y, X)
failure_modes.cause: Cross-covariance is generally rectangular and not symmetric; cov(X, Y) has dimension m x n whereas cov(Y, X) has dimension n x m
